rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods, Experiments 1-4 on the Ushkonyr demonstration site, 2012/2013-2016, three replications, plots 14-50 sq.m. Q2: Table 13 and Results: rice under surface/subsurface drip irrigation with mulching film yielded 52.4/43.2 c/ha on average versus 26.2 c/ha under flooding; Table 8 shows higher productive tillering and grains per panicle under drip with film; Conclusions state that drip irrigation with mulching film promotes early and uniform emergence of rice and soybean shoots, intensive growth and higher productivity; soybean yield of 42.2 c/ha with film and higher yield in mulch variants than without mulch. Q7: Results (Table 13 text): drip plots without mulching film were overrun by weeds and growth stopped at booting, so the film was required and non-film variants were dropped; Conclusions: optimum irrigating norm 4-6 thousand m3/ha with evening/night watering; Discussion: in the variable climate of south-east Kazakhstan the film is a necessity for soybean. Q9: Table 17 reports soybean yield-structure and biological harvest as mean <U+00B1> m (standard error); Tables 13-16 give experimental error P% and LSD0.95.
rows.notes: The emergence effect specifically is stated only in the abstract/conclusions; field germination was counted (methods) but no emergence data table is shown, so Q2 rests mainly on yield and yield-structure data for drip-with-film versus flooding. Q4: mechanisms (soil temperature, moisture retention under film) are asserted, not measured for rice/soybean; the nutrient data in Table 7 are from sugarbeet plots. Q5: single site, two crops. Q6: plot-scale (0.04-0.6 ha experiments). Q8: the only comment on small plot size is a justification (cost of equipment), not a stated limitation of results; the note that efficiency of drip ways was ambiguous across years is not framed as a limitation.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods, field experiments 2012-2016 at Ushkonyr, weed infestation recorded by standard methodical instructions (Astana 2004). Q2: Results (text to Table 13): drip irrigation plots without mulching film became overgrown with weeds and mechanical/chemical control was ineffective, whereas plots with film yielded 43-52 c/ha; Conclusions: drip irrigation with mulching film reduces weed infestation of rice 8-10 times, allowing manual, mechanical and chemical weed control to be excluded; for soybean the most effective weed control was drip irrigation under mulch film, with weeds in early season not exceeding 36-44 plants/m2; Discussion: three-year studies showed mulching film under drip suspends weed growth in rice and soybean.
rows.notes: The weed-suppression result is reported only as summary statements (8-10 fold reduction; 36-44 weeds/m2) without a data table or dispersion measure. The comparison is essentially drip-with-film versus drip-without-film and flooding, which matches the combined DIPM technology in the passage. Q4: the proposed mechanism (localized wetting) is asserted, not measured. Q7: the only condition stated is that the mulching film must be present, which is inherent to the DIPM technology itself, so not counted. Q9: '36-44 units/m2' is an upper bound rather than a dispersion measure.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a translated Kazakh field study with weak reporting: several conclusions (emergence, weed reduction, soil nitrogen regime) are stated without supporting tables; agrophysical/agrochemical tables partly concern sugarbeet and oats plots rather than rice/soybean.
